power. 
Suggested Purpose: Render inert things/beings of great 
danger or power. 
Suggested Destruction Method:  If the trunk is taken to 
the abyss and opened and then a gateway to the abyss itself 
is made within the trunk, it will consume itself and all 
contents, forever.  
Anomalies: Living things that enter the trunk fall into a 
state of suspended animation, they become inert and lifeless 
but they are not dead, just unable to function, act, think, and 
are held in this state until removed. Deities and beings with 
a 30 Will Force are able to move and act normally within the 
trunk and leave whenever they wish. Dimensional items can 
be placed within the trunk and even each other while in the 
trunk without ill effects. When removed they automatically 
separate. 
Base Aura Level 30
Abilities (item only, no Aura required)
Dimension (The internal size of the trunk is 1 mile long, 1 
half a mile wide and 1 mile deep), Invulnerability (constant), 
Inscrutable (constant), Size Change (trunk can grow or shrink 
as needed without altering the internal size of the trunk.) 
Powers (activated at will, no Aura Control required)
Teleportation (any object placed in the top of the trunk, 
teleports to the surface within and back out as desired by 
whoever is using it)
Inscrutable (anything placed within the trunk cannot be 
sensed, found, etc.)
Mastery Requirement: Desire to protect someone or the 
world from the negative effects of a dangerous person or 
thing, then placing the person or thing within the trunk.  
Mastery Powers: Magical and divine effects of items do not 
operate while they are in the trunk, save for some artifacts.
Exp. Value: 15,250	
Gp. Value: 75,000

Aetherwart
Type: Fungus spores
Climate: Ethereal Plane
Magical: Yes
Value: 1-2 platinum
Potency: indefinite if kept in the sealed spore pod.
Duration: The spores can be kept indefinitely but once 
released from their pod they whither in 1 week. 
Preparation/Usage: carefully seal and then remove the filled 
spore pod.  Squeeze the pod to release the spores either 
into a cloud that is inhaled or into something that will be 
ingested. 
Powers: Magic Resistance is reduced by 25% for 1 day. If the 
being dies while affected, Aetherwart fungus will spout on 
the corpse in 24 hours and have 1d10+10 mature (full) spore 
pods within a week. 
Description: A gray, somewhat translucent fungus that 
grows on dead beings and creatures feeding off of their dissi-
pating auras. When the fungus blooms it then becomes dor-
mant bursting when the dead being is touched or disturbed. 
The spores are small and stick to any warn surface, fur or a 
living body for example.

Type: Flower
Climate: Plane of Earth (and Fae)
Magical: Yes
Value: 1-3 platinum
Potency: Constant, as long as roots are nourished
Duration: 0 minutes if removed from roots
Preparation/Usage: Come within the flower’s illumination
Powers: Heals all wounded areas up to 50 points of damage, 
once every 10 seconds.  Once an Angelwing has healed a 
total of 2000 points of damage, its light fades and its blossom 
shrivels and dies.
Description: Extremely rare, these flowers grow to be 2d4’ 
tall.  Each stem is as thick as a small tree, and its leaves are 
1d4’ long.  The flowers themselves consist of 7 long, drap-
ing white leaves bearing a silver shimmering sheen.  Each 
flower glows with a soothing white light.  These flowers are 
typically found in sparse clusters of 1d4 blossoms every 100 
square miles.  If the blossom is removed from its roots, its 
light instantly fades.

Climate: Plane of Death

Anyone entering the fog must make a half Vitality save or 
become nauseated, resulting in -5 to hit and +5 to Initiative.

Type: Leaf, root, seed
Climate: Plane of Earth
Magical: Yes
Value: 1-2 platinum

• The oxygen amount in the air and water is halved, and

reaching down to the lake bed.  Hairy roots spread outward 
and sprout one new daughter plant every 2 hours.  There-
fore, vast colonies of King’s Hyacinth can spread over many 
miles if not contained.  
Notes: A separate successful Herb Lore skill relays knowl-
edge of King’s Hyacinth mundane cousin, Water Hyacinth, 
which also purifies water yet draws oxygen from it, grows at 
a rather quick rate, and can cause mild itching.  King’s Hy-
acinth is a much more detrimental, magical variety of that 
common invasive flower.

Spiritseed (Seed)
Type: Seed
Climate: Plane of Life
Magical: Yes
Value: 4-7 platinum
Potency: Eternal
Duration: 10 minutes
Preparation/Usage: Breathed upon by a living being.
Powers: Opens a portal to the Plane of Life, with a 10% 
chance of a Life Elemental to appear.  Treat any resulting 
elementals as cast at Aura 19, as per the spell or invocation 
Summon Life Elemental.  This portal takes 10 minutes 
to form, and once an elemental appears, it remains until 
banished.  Each Spiritseed is dissolved by the user’s breath.
Description: Small translucent seed found inside a Spirit-
seed nut.  Each Spiritseed tree produces 2d10 walnut-sized 
nuts, and each nut contains 1 seed.  5d4 doses are usually 
found.
Spiritseed (Tree)
Type: Tree
Climate: Plane of Life
Magical: Yes
Value: 1-4 platinum (per lb.)
Potency: Eternal
Duration: See below
Preparation/Usage: See below
Powers: Grows Spiritseed nuts and is +4 magical wood with 
Finger of Life.
Description: The Spiritseed tree reaches a height of 3-6’ 
and is translucent silver.  Instead of leaves, the tree produces 
2d10 walnut-sized, translucent nuts.  Upon the tree’s outer 
surface lies a silvery sheen of Life energy, inflicting 6d4 
damage to any undead or negative life force beings to the 
body area touching the tree, as well as 1d4 adjacent body ar-
eas if a Magic Resistance is made, and destruction if a Magic 
Resistance at -6% is failed.  It also heals 6d4 to the body area 
touched, as well as 1d4 adjacent body areas, for any living or 
positive life force beings.  If a corpse touches the tree within 
6 minutes of death, he may make a half Will Force save to 
be resurrected.  Even if this roll is failed, if the skills Resur-
rection, Recover, or True Recovery is begun on the deceased 
within 3 minutes, the being may make a new Will Force save 
with a bonus of +3% to be resurrected and permanently 
loses 1 Will Force.
Notes: Wood Lore may be used on a Spiritseed tree to trans-
fer the power of Finger of Life.  If using Spiritseed wood to 

===== PAGE 520 =====
514
produce a weapon or piece of armor, this power remains 
as well, though obviously any undead wielding it should 
protect themselves with an immunity to Life damage.  Any 
weapons or armor made of this wood is considered +4 wood 
with an Object Strength and Armor Value of 28.
Spying Lady
Type: Flower
Climate: Plane of Water
Magical: Yes
Value: 2-5 platinum
Potency: 1 week
Duration: Constant
Preparation/Usage: Hold blossom up to ear.
Powers: Allows someone to listen in on one person, place, 
or thing on the user’s current plane, as if their sense of 
hearing was within hearing of the person, place, or thing. 
The user must state his target’s name aloud.  Beings with 
Non-Detection, Sphere of Protection, Wall of Protection, 
Mind Set, Mind Change, Silence, or Thought Projection 
cannot be detected, and beings with Life Sense or Sense 
Projection (or similar effects) are given an Intelligence save 
to feel they are being eavesdropped upon.
Description: A 5” wide blossom whose 2 large rounded pet-
als curve around the center to form a deep bowl.  The petals 
are bright yellow with tiny red splotches, and the style is 
long and yellow with a bulbous stigma.  These flowers grow 
on a dark green vine with heart-shaped leaves and hangs 
from cliffs or spreads along rocky shores.  Each bowl-shaped 
blossom holds the power to Eavesdrop.  This flower cannot 
be dried, since its power fades when it dies.
Notes: Beings who are around the user will hear no sound 
coming from the flower.
Star Violet
Type: Flower
Climate: Plane of Earth
Magical: Yes
Value: 2-4 platinum
Potency: 1 hour
Duration: 1d4+1 hours
Preparation/Usage: Pollen inhaled deeply
Powers: Grants immunity to the user’s mind against 
mental attacks, control, effects of insanity, or converting 
to a mental-only form of undead, such as a Horror.  If the 
user is already insane or controlled, then these effects are 
temporarily removed.  Furthermore, mental attributes are 
protected from being drained involuntarily. The user cannot 
themselves engage in mental combat or contact another 
being telepathically, nor can they be mentally contacted or 
probed by others while the herb is in effect.
Description: A plant with a stem 2d4’ tall and leaves 
1d20+4” long, whose flowers have five petals the shade of 
pale lavender in the center, gradually darkening to deep pur-
ple at the tips.  In the center spring a mass of bright yellow 
stamen.  Each root system will produce 1d4 individual stems 
with its own blossom.  Star violets bloom for 100 years, after 
which it begins to fade and dies within 1d4 hours.  Each 
dose consists of a whole blossom.  Upon sensing its pollen 
being inhaled, the flower will continue to emit every last 
spore.  If the user fails to breathe in all the pollen, he be-
comes dizzy for 2d10 seconds, resulting in an Agility save or 
falling down, but no magical effect occurs.
Sunfruit
Type: Fruit
Climate: Plane of Time
Magical: Yes
Value: 2-4 platinum
Potency: 1 week, x6 if dried
Duration: Instant
Preparation/Usage: Ingested.
Powers: Restores personal attributes that were lost 
involuntarily.  Each attribute point returns at a rate of 1 per 
hour.
Description: A peach-sized round fruit the shade of yel-
lowish-orange, which grows on a smooth-barked white tree.  
Each tree consists of 3d20 ripe fruit.  Each bite restores 1 
personal attribute.
Thornblaze
Type: Thorn
Climate: Plane of Fire
Magical: Yes
Value: 2-5 platinum
Potency: 6 weeks, x6 if dried
Duration: 1d4 hours
Preparation/Usage: Touched, or take at least 1 point of 
damage.
Powers: +2d4 Will Force for the duration when touched, 
but also inflicts 2d6 magical fire damage unless a Magic 
Resistance is made.  Its thorns inflict 1d4 thrusting damage, 
and anyone who takes 1 point of damage from thorns 
must make an Illusion Resistance or feel incredibly painful 

===== PAGE 521 =====
515
burning as the thorn’s power enters the bloodstream and 
flows throughout her body.  If this resistance is failed, the 
user is incapacitated and must make a Vitality save every 
minute or fall unconscious for the duration.
Description: A twisted, leafless black vine swirling with red 
flames.  Its thorns are 2” long and inflict 1d4 thrusting dam-
age if an Agility save is failed when handling the vine.
Notes: Weapon Making or Armor Making may be used to 
apply the thorns to a weapon or piece of armor, in which 
case they retain all powers until their potency has worn off.
Tombseed (Seed)
Type: Seed
Climate: Plane of Death
Magical: Yes
Value: 4-7 platinum
Potency: Eternal
Duration: 10 minutes
Preparation/Usage: Placed inside a corpse that died within 
the past 10 minutes.
Powers: Opens a portal to the Plane of Death, with a 10% 
chance of a Death Elemental to appear.  Treat any resulting 
elementals as cast at Aura 19, as per the spell or invocation 
Summon Death Elemental.  This portal takes 10 minutes 
to form, and once an elemental appears, it remains until 
banished.  Each Tombseed is dissolved by the corpse in 
which it was placed.
Description: Small black seed found inside a Tombseed nut. 
Each Tombseed tree produces 2d10 walnut-sized nuts, and 
each nut contains 1 seed.  5d4 doses are usually found.
Tombseed (Tree)
Type: Tree
Climate: Plane of Death
Magical: Yes
Value: 1-4 platinum (per lb.)
Potency: Eternal
Duration: See below
Preparation/Usage: See below
Powers: Grows Tombseed nuts and is +4 magical wood with 
Finger of Death.
Description: The Tombseed tree reaches a height of 3-6’ and 
is glistening black.  Instead of leaves, the tree produces 2d10 
walnut-sized, pure black nuts.  Upon the tree’s outer surface 
lies a dark translucent sheen of Death energy, inflicting 6d4 
damage to any living or positive life force beings to the body 
area touching the tree, as well as 1d4 adjacent body areas if 
a Magic Resistance is made, and death if a Magic Resistance 
at -6% is failed.  It also heals 6d4 to the body area touched, 
as well as 1d4 adjacent areas, for any undead or negative life 
force beings.  If a living target dies from this effect, there is 
a 15% chance he will rise as an appropriate undead of the 
Game Master’s choice.  The target may resist this with a Will 
Force save at -12%. 
Notes: Wood Lore may be used on a Tombseed tree to 
transfer the power of Finger of Death.  If using Tombseed 
wood to produce a weapon or piece of armor, this power 
remains as well, though obviously those wielding it should 
protect themselves with an immunity to death damage.  Any 
weapons or armor made of this wood is considered +4 wood 
with an Object Strength and Armor Value of 28.
Trance Thistle
Type: Flower
Climate: Plane of Dreams
Magical: Yes
Value: 2-5 platinum
Potency: 1 week, x6 if dried
Duration: 10 minutes
Preparation/Usage: Watch or ingest.
Powers: Transfixes any who catch sight of the plant for 
10 minutes, unless a Control Resistance is made.  Anyone 
so affected must stare at the plant for the duration, 
having no other actions.  They do, however, get a new 
Control Resistance each 10 seconds.  If line of sight 
contact is broken, the affected beings are freed from 
this entrancement, but the released creature must make 
another Control Resistance if they look at the plant again 
or be entranced.  Upon ingesting any part of the plant, the 
user falls into a meditative trance for 10 minutes, during 
which he will experience 2d4 premonitions of himself and/
or others.  During this state and afterward, the following 
benefits apply:
• A new Control Resistance towards any current 
controlling factors and a +10% Control Resistance.
• +1 to hit and damage for 1 hour after the herb’s duration.
• Current fatigue effects are reduced by ½.  Fatigue effects 
for the duration happen twice as slowly (1 minute of 
fatigue is applied per 2 actual minutes).
• One temporarily lost attribute point is restored per 30 
minutes while awake, and one per 10 minutes while asleep.
• The user counts as having 1 Will Force rating higher 
when defending against a hostile spell or effect which 
depends on Will Force, such as mental combat, the spell 
and invocation Hold, Possession, etc.
Description: A thistle-like plant with scintillating blossoms 
of all colors, that can reach a height of 1d6+1’.  The entire 

===== PAGE 522 =====
516
plant is soft and mushy to the touch, and handfuls can 
be scooped from any part of the plant with little effort.  It 
continuously sways in a mesmerizing dance.  Although its 
thistle-like leaves appear sharp and thorny, its soft mushy 
quality makes it completely harmless to the touch.
Troll's Hair
Type: Grass
Climate: Plane of Death
Magical: Yes
Value: 1-2 platinum
Potency: 4 weeks, x6 if dried
Duration: 1d4 days
Preparation/Usage: Dried and ground, then ingested or 
enters bloodstream.
Powers: -1d4 Vitality and Agility, causes 3 levels of fatigue, 
and prevents the user from being healed in any way, unless a 
Poison Resistance is made.
Description: A tall, grayish-green grass that grows up to 3’ 
tall in areas up to 50’ wide.  One dose is 1 oz of powder.  The 
powder can be mixed with a liquid with the intention of 
either drinking or applying to a weapon as poison.
Twisted Roperoot
Type: Vine
Climate: Plane of Death
Magical: Yes
Value: 2-5 platinum
Potency: 6 weeks, x3 if dried
Duration: 2d4 hours
Preparation/Usage: Worn or held.
Powers: Protects an undead, death elemental, etc., from the 
damage caused by life/positive based powers, skills, spells, 
and effects.  Thus, the effects that cause damage, blinding, 
burns, etc. from positive or life-based attacks have no 
effect on the protected undead.  This does not stop turning, 
banishment, or destruction based positive/life effects.  
Furthermore, this vine grants immunity to all beings from 
the effects of pressure in water and in lava, as well as the 
benefits of Endure Heat, Endure Cold, and Breathless.
Description: A gnarled, twisted black vine with razor-edged 
leaves which inflict 2d4 cutting unless an Agility save is 
made when handling the plant.  The vine itself is 1” thick.  
When worn openly, Twisted Roperoot will cut through 
cloth, leather, skin, fur, etc., with a 10% chance of each leaf 
doing damage every minute.  It is recommended to store 
this in a protective container or to wear appropriately resis-
tant clothing.
Vaporleaf
Type: Leaf
Climate: Plane of Air
Magical: Yes
Value: 1-4 platinum
Potency: 1 month, x8 if dried
Duration: 2 hours
Preparation/Usage: Ground and burned on an incense 
stick.
Powers: Creates a magical wind to blow in the direction the 
incense stick is pointing. This wind has a constant speed of 
50 miles per hour for as long as the incense is burning.
Description: A translucent green oak-like leaf growing on a 
slender white tree reaching a height of 2d20’.  Its course bark 
grows in swirling patterns.  Each dose is 1 oz. of powdered 
leaf.
Vitalia
Type: Flower
Climate: Plane of Life
Magical: Yes
Value: 1-3 platinum
Potency: Eternal
Duration: Eternal
Preparation/Usage: Held or worn.
Powers: Grants immunity to the effects of pressure in water 
and lava, as well as the benefits of Endure Death, Endure 
Heat, Endure Cold, and Breathless.
Description: An incredibly rare rose bush whose translu-
cent blossoms, stem, and leaves are faintly tinged with blue-
green.  This plant can easily be mistaken for crystal when 
first seen, but it is surprisingly supple to the touch.  Each 
rose can reach a width of 3” and must be attached to at least 
9” of stem and at least 3 leaves to contain its magic.  Each 
bush produces 1d4 doses.

Wanderstalk
Type: See below
Climate: Plane of the Lost
Magical: Yes
Value: 1-3 platinum
Potency: 2d4 minutes
Duration: Eternal
Preparation/Usage: Touched, then held or worn.
Powers: -1d4 Knowledge when first touched, unless a Magic

a piece at least 6” long, he and everything he is carrying 
will be teleported every 1d4x10 minutes to a random 
location within 100’.  A Magic Resistance is allowed for each 
teleportation.
Description: Every 2d4 minutes, this plant molds itself into 
various bushes, saplings, vines, mushrooms, and flowers 
no larger than 4 cubic feet.  Each piece held or worn by a 
being continues to mold shape every 2d4 minutes, assuming 
the form of any similar-sized object of which the user has 
knowledge.  When the user drops or puts down the piece 
of Wanderstalk, it will affect the next being who touches 
it within the next 2d4 minutes.  If nobody has touched it 
by then, it shifts into its natural form, a dead weed, and its 
magic fades.

Witherwhiff
Type: Flower
Climate: Plane of Air
Magical: Yes
Value: 1-2 platinum
Potency: 1 week
Duration: 2d4+1 hours
Preparation/Usage: Touched, then worn or held.
Powers: Contains a static shield around it, stunning

Resistance is made. This static shield endures indefinitely 
while planted and for 1 week after being picked. A being 
must only make a new Magic Resistance if it leaves his Aura 
field and he attempts to touch it again.  Anyone wearing or 
holding a Witherwhiff blossom will gain this static shield. 
Furthermore, the blossom also has a 2’ radius air pocket 
around it full of breathable oxygen, but anyone inside the 
air pocket has a -2d4 Appearance, and all objects appear old 
and covered in rust or dirt.
Description: A 2’ tall leafy plant whose flowers have 5

Check allows for recognition of tiny electrical currents zap-
ping from one stamen to the next. Each flower holds these

Wild Scarlytte
Type: Flower
Climate: Plane of Dreams
Magical: Yes
Value: 1-3 platinum
Potency: 1 week, x6 if dried
Duration: 3d4 hours
Preparation/Usage: Ingested or dried, ground, and smoked.

Wishberry
Type: Berry
Climate: Plane of Dreams
Magical: Yes
Value: 1-3 platinum
Potency: Eternal
Duration: See below
Preparation/Usage: Ingested whole or diluted into water 
and drunk as juice.
Powers: Induces a deep magical sleep.  The user is allowed 
a Control Resistance if unwilling or unaware.  During sleep, 
the user dreams 1d4 slightly varying dreams depicting 
her fondest wish.  Each dream lasts 6d10+10 seconds 
and is clearly remembered after awakening.  Each dose of 
Wishberry permanently lowers Intelligence and Wisdom 
ratings by 1.  This berry is highly addictive, and the user 
must make a Will Force save not to take a second dose 
within the next full day.  If a second dose is taken, she must 
make Will Force saves at a cumulative -5% every 12 hours 
to not take further doses.  Once the user succumbs and 
takes another dose, her Will Force save resets to full, but the 
process continues as before.  This addiction may be cured 
with the invocation Cure (5% chance per Piety Control) or 
the skill Cure Disease made at -30%.
Description: A ripe, juicy berry appearing to each individ-
ual as their favorite color, growing on a leafy, vibrant bush 
that reaches a height of 3-6’.  Each bush produces 5d20x5 
berries, and each berry is 1 dose.
Witch's Cap
Type: Mushroom
Climate: Plane of Dreams
Magical: Yes
Value: 2-5 platinum
Potency: 3 weeks, x6 if dried
Duration: 2d4 hours
Preparation/Usage: Touched and ingested.
Powers: Allows one user who ingests half the mushroom to 
shroud his mind in a near complete mental copy of another 
user who holds the mushroom’s other half.  Whenever 
anyone mentally contacts the being who ingested, they 
sense the duplicated mind and not his actual mind.  If the

519
one who ingested engages or is engaged in mental combat 
or a strong mental connection with another being, then 
the herb’s effect immediately fails.  The being who ingested 
is allowed a double Perception Check to receive thoughts, 
emotions, and details from the being holding the other half 
of the mushroom that he was thinking and feeling at the 
time of mental duplication.
Description: A deep purple, pointed fungi that can reach a 
height of 2d6” and grow in clusters of 1d6 individuals.  Each

mental duplication of one being to another.  This can be 
accomplished with a Mathematics skill or half Intelligence 
save.

Climate: Plane of Water
Magical: Yes
Value: 1-3 platinum

Duration: See below
Preparation/Usage: Touched.

Wormroot
Type: Root
Climate: Plane of Earth
Magical: Yes
Value: 3-7 platinum
Potency: 3 weeks, x6 if dried
Duration: 2d4 hours
Preparation/Usage: Dried, ground, and added to a magical

Wraith Heart
Type: Berry
Climate: Plane of Death
Magical: Yes
Value: 2-4 platinum
Potency: 3 weeks
Duration: 2d4 minutes
Preparation/Usage: Squeezed or crushed until berry bursts.
Powers: Creates a 20’ wide sphere of suffocating darkness 
which negates all forms of vision.  All beings within the 
sphere begin to choke, losing 1d6 overall Endurance per 
10 seconds.  At the onset of asphyxiation, a Will Force 
save must be made to remain calm or damage is doubled.  
When Endurance has been reduced to 0, a being appears 
very pale and must make a Vitality save every 5 seconds to 
remain conscious (-5% to the save for every point below 0).  
Once Endurance reaches a being’s negative Vitality rating, 
the lungs have collapsed and the heart stops beating.  One 
minute later, if Endurance is not raised above the negative 
Vitality rating, the being dies.  A Chirugeon roll will 
resuscitate the suffocated being and raise overall Endurance 
to 1 point above negative Vitality.  Should a being survive 
the ordeal, restoration of Endurance is based on the healing 
rate of the character, with minutes instead of days and a 
period of 10-minute intervals instead of weeks. If the being 
dies from suffocation, he has a 100% chance minus his Will 
Force rating of returning as a physical undead within 10 
minutes of death.
Description: Appears as a dull black cherry growing on a 
gnarled black tree.  A Perception check allows a being to 
notice the surface of each cherry swirling with a faint, sickly 
green mist.

New Potions
Masking Body: (Optional Exp. Value: 250)  
Effects: Appear in an alternate illusionary form per the spells 
Illusion of Sight, Smell, Sound, Taste, Touch.  
Duration: 1d4+1 hours.
Masking Mind: (Optional Exp. Value: 250)  
Effects: Appear to have an alternate mind per the spell 
Illusion of Feeling when mentally contacted, also acts as the 
spell Mind Set unless an Illusion Resistance is requested and 
made. 
Duration: 1d4+1 hours.
Non-Detection: (Optional Exp. Value: 300)  
Effects: acts as the spell Non-Detection for the duration. 
Duration: 2d4+2 hours.
Plane Shifting: (Optional Exp. Value: 500)  
Effects: projects the spirit of the drinker onto an open 
plane of their choice. The drinker’s body remains in repose, 
breathing but otherwise unmoving for the duration. 
Duration: 2d4+2 hours.
Shadow Walking: (Optional Exp. Value: 200)  
Effects: Physically shifts the drinker unto the Plane of 
Shadow. The user remains there until the duration expires 
then is returned to their plane of origin. This potion will not 
work unless the Shadow Plane is accessible from the current 
plane.  
Duration: 2d4+2 hours.
Sleeping Potion (Strong): (Optional Exp. Value: 50)  
Effects: Causes the imbiber to make a Magic Resistance 
or fall into a deep, unwaking dreamless sleep. The victim 
cannot be woken save by magical or divine effects. The 
victim is also sustained as the Sustenance invocation 
needing neither food nor water and Breathless as the spell, 
appearing to be in a near suspended state, though the victim 
still ages. 
Duration: Until waken by magic or divinity. 
New Potion Recipes 
Masking Body: (viscous opaque pink potion)
•	 1/2 pint of water from (The Dreamscape.)
•	 1/2 pint of Changeling (blood.)
•	 2 ounces of ground Fool’s Ear (herb.)
•	 Tuft of Fur (ground) from a Gwe or Gwegar.
Mix blood and water and bring to a boil. Then slowly stir in 
the Fool’s Ear before just as it boils. Reduce heat and add fur. 
Cook for 1 hour. 
Masking Mind: (viscous opaque purple potion)
•	 1/2 pint of water from (the dreamscape.)
•	 1/2 pint of Doppelganger (blood.)
•	 2 ounces of ground Fool’s Ear (herb.)
•	 Tuft of Fur (ground) from a Gwe or Gwegar.
Mix blood and water and bring to a boil. 
Then slowly stir in the fur just as it boils. Reduce heat and 
add Fool’s Ear. Cover, simmer for 6 hours, then pour before 
it congeals. 
Non-Detection: (completely clear potion)
•	 1/2 pint of water from (The Plane of Water or the Astral 
Sea.)
•	 1/2 pint of blessed or magical water. 
•	 2 ounces of used Fadegrass herb.
•	 4 Tears of any Fae. 
Begin with the blessed/magical water. Freeze the water and 
then add ice produced to the water from the Plane of Water/
Astral Sea. As the ice melts add in the Fadegrass and the 
tears. Wait for Fadegrass leaves to sink into the water and 
vanish. When this occurs (usually in about an hour) quickly 
pour and cap the potion. 
Plane Shifting: (blue potion with swirling silvery particles)
•	 1 pint of water from (The Plane of Water or the Astral 
Sea.)
•	 1 ground unused Thunderseed (herb.)
•	 2 ounces of Djinn or Ifrit saliva.
Distill the water until pure. Add the saliva and bring to 
a boil. Immediately lower to a simmer and add ground 
Thunderseed. Continue to simmer, stirring occasionally for 
2 hours. Pour and cap. 
Shadow Walking: (murky, swirling black and gray potion)
•	 1/2 pint of unholy or magical water. 
•	 1/2 pint of Fade Cat blood.
•	 2 ounces of Detractor Wisp dust.
•	 6 ounces of ground undead bone. 
Begin at midnight on a night with no visible moon (or in a 
darkened room). Add the Detractor Wisp dust to the water 
and stir for 1 hour. Freeze for 1 day. Allow to thaw. Stir in 
the blood while it thaws. When it has completely thawed 
add the ground undead bone and stir for another hour. Pour 
and cap. 
Sleeping Potion (Strong): (viscous gray potion)
•	 1 pint of water from (the dreamscape.)
•	 1 drop of nightmare poison from any dream. creature 
that produces it. 
•	 3 ounces of stone shavings from a Preserver.
•	 3 ounces of ground thorns of a black rose. 
Start with the shavings and thorns. Sift these together and 
then shake thoroughly until they are a near uniform gray. 
Then heat the water but do not boil it. Stir in the shavings 1 
ounce per hour for six hours. Begin freeze. Add poison drop 
just before the last of the mixture freezes. Cover and allow to 
thaw. Bottle next midnight and cap.

Recipes for Existing Potions
Endure Light: (glowing yellow potion)
•	 1/2 pint of blessed or magical water. 
•	 1/2 pint of Sustasphere pulp.
•	 6 ounces of ground sunflower seeds. 
•	 1 pinch of desert sand ground fine. 
•	 1 tip of a Giant Owl feather. 
Must be prepared in open daylight. Carefully pull the giant 
feather tip apart until each piece is a single strand. Add in 
ground sunflower seeds and place in open container in the 
sun at high noon. Begin boiling the water. After reaching 
a boil reduce heat to just below boiling and pour in desert 
sand. Gather the feather/seed mix and now add in the pulp 
from the Sustasphere. Slowly scoop this viscous mix into the 
near boiling water one heaping spoonful at a time. Slowly 
lower heat to be off as the sun sets. Just as the sun disappears 
over the horizon, bottle and cap. 
Endure Magic/Aura: (glowing blue potion)
•	 1/2 pint of water exposed to a magical mishap. 
•	 1 ounces of the blood of any magical humanoid. 
•	 1 ground ounce of any planar herb (unused.) 
•	 1 pinch of any ground magical metal. 
Warm the blood, add in the ground magical metal and 
simmer. Separately warm the water and add the ground 
herb while simmering. Every 10 minutes pour a spoonful of 
one mixture into the other and vice versa. Continue for four 
hours. At the end of this period pour both warm mixtures 
together and boil until it glows blue. Bottle and cap. 
Endure Poison: (lime green potion)
•	 1 pint of water blessed or magical water. 
•	 2 drops of any magical animal poison. 
•	 1 ground ounce of any herbal poison. 
•	 6 ounces of congealed blood of a magical humanoid who 
died of poisoning.
Start with the water. Bring to a boil. Quickly put in the two 
kinds of poison. Distill and repour the distilled purification 
back into the remains and repeat three times. Take the final 
distillation and discard the remnants. Pour in the congealed 
blood, stirring until suspension is achieved.  Freeze 
overnight. Thaw in the light of a new day. When the mixture 
is half thawed, carefully remove the remainder of frozen 
mixture. Set this in a container and discard the previous 
thaw. Heat the frozen mixture and pour into container 
through a fine sieve. Bottle and cap. 
Endure Sound: (barely blue translucent potion)
•	 1 pint of water from Rockholm.
•	 8 ear hairs of any Fae. 
•	 2 ounces of Marid saliva. 
Boil the water. Add the saliva and simmer. Reduce heat 
slowly over 2 hours and drop in 1 ear hair every 15 minutes. 
Bottle cold and cap. 
Enhancing Taste: (viscous orange/yellow potion)
•	 1/2 pint of blessed water.
•	 3 ground Treasure Berry (herb) seeds.
•	 1/4 pint of Dwarven whiskey.
•	 1/4 pint of Elven wine. 
Mix everything together as quickly as possible. Alternately 
boil and freeze the mixture three times and then let thaw in 
a closed container overnight. Bottle and cap in the morning 
light. 
Enhancing Touch: (viscous brown/yellow potion)
•	 1 pint of Grent or Wakewood Sap. 
•	 6 ounces of Giant Bee honey.
•	 2 ounces of Fade Cat, Gwe, or Gwegar saliva.
•	 1 pinch of any ground magical stone or gem. 
Heat the sap until it flows. Fold in the honey. Bring to a 
slow boil. Sprinkle in the ground stone/gem while boiling. 
Reduce heat, simmer for 1 hour. Bring back to a boil and 
pour in the saliva. Remove from heat. While still hot and 
pourable, bottle and cap. 
Mental Power: (silver potion with blue flakes)
•	 1 pint of water from the Astral Sea.
•	 6 ounces of ground high grade Mithreel. 
•	 3 ounces of Xar’Vell/Gray Shadow Flayer brain. 
•	 3 ounces of Psychoworm Blood. 
Marinate the Brain overnight in the Blood. Braise the brain 
until golden brown. Poor the remainder of the marinade 
onto the brain as cooking. Dice the brain fine. Set aside. Boil 
the water slowly stirring in in the metallic powder. Add in 
the diced brain. Reduce heat, simmer for 2 hours. Carefully 
pour off the mixture so that the heaviest powders remain 
and only the light flakes and floating bits make it into the 
mixture. Shake the mixture continuously until the material 
suspends completely. Bottle and cap. 
Protection, Dragons: (clear potion with silver flakes)
•	 1 pint of dragon saliva.
•	 1 pinch of ground dragon scale. 
•	 3 ounces of Dao, Djinn, Ifrit, or Marid blood.
•	 3 ounces of eye fluid from an Eye of Fire, Terror, or 
Torment.
Mix the blood and eye fluid together in a closed container. 
Heat until the blood congeals. Poor into the dragon saliva 
and cover immediately. Bring to a boil covered. Open 
quickly and drop in the pinch of ground scale. Simmer and 
mix thoroughly for three hours. Bottle just below boiling, 
and cap.

Telekinesis: (translucent red potion)
•	 1 pint of water from the Astral Sea. 
•	 1 Giant Owl feather.
•	 2 ounces of Storm (or Cloud) Giant blood.
•	 2 ounces of dried White Shroud spores.
Carefully pull apart the feather into individual strips. Dice 
the strips to make small motes. Discard the remaining quill.

until the feathers are brownish red. Begin boiling the water.

a boil. Reduce the heat to a simmer and slowly shake the

lightly red pour through a fine sieve, bottle and cap.

525
Game Mastering
High Title (Epic) Game Mastering
There is inherent risk when running epic, high title games. The first of these is that the players themselves should 
be well familiar with their characters and how they work to achieve their goals. There is sometimes a desire to 
rush to the “good stuff” and start out with powerful characters in the thick of it. Doing this would be especially 
dangerous in Imagine as characters can take a while to feel out how the skill abilities work and what is effective 
and what not so in given situations. If you desire to play a higher title game, ease into it. Play first through the 
lower titles, maybe even more than once so that the players become not only familiar with the general rules 
but experienced enough to appreciate the intricacies and dangers of a high title game. These epic adventures 
can span many, sessions or explode spectacularly changing the setting forever. In this section we will deal with 
initiation, preparation, consultation and then the play itself and its aftermath and a final warning.
Initiation: Somewhere between 8th and 10th title characters generally reach their natural conclusions. They now 
have followers, duties to others and often settle down into non-adventuring roles they have earned as pillars of 
the community, masters of estates, and/or just raising families. This is to be encouraged. If there is any way to 
“win” a role playing game it is the earning of an important (non-adventuring) place in the society they were born 
into or even establishing new settlements and leading them to success. This natural endgame is explored more in 
the next section on strongholds. Yet, there are times when the party has a sense that there is more to do. When 
instead of settling down, living in an estate built from the riches they have earned, they wish to go on. Perhaps 
the party desires to take on the tasks that are too much for mere mortals; the works of the very gods themselves, 
or to travel the planes and become part of an even greater culture; the society of immortals and planar denizens. 
Doing so often means leaving the earthly realms, but even when staying, their concerns grow so that their 
connection to normal beings is strained and their purposes are beyond the petty dangers of early adventuring 
life. If the party seems strongly desirous of continuing their adventures, with the proper preparation and focus 
epic, high-title adventures can be the stuff of legends; tales that will be told to each other and their gaming 
friends for a long time to come. Just make sure they and you are ready to take on the challenge. World changing, 
or ending events can be in the offing and you are leaving it to other players to determine the fate of the setting 
you will have spent a great deal of time crafting. 
Preparation: To be ready for an epic, high title game you must flesh out what the great conflicts are. These will be 
the ones that mortals sense from a distance. There are many examples and these are but a few: That two gods are 
vying for dominion over one or more cultures. Perhaps one plane is corrupting and influencing another, taking it 
over subtly at first and then overtly as great rift wars begin. A cataclysm is coming and it needs to be stopped or 
at the very least prepared for if the spark of civilization has any chance to continue. Create a list of the all of these 
great conflicts. Use the previous adventures the characters have had as inspiration. If they have fought against 
the minions of dark gods then weave the larger narrative about the god’s efforts to change the moral realm so 
that his strength grows and others lessens. Flesh out the dark god’s greatest agents in all the realms the characters 
will venture into, his high priests in the earthly realms, his supernatural servants in the planar realms and even 
his current exarch. If you have not completely fleshed out the dark god, the motivations, powers, spheres of 
influence, devotions (invocations areas), etc., take time to do so now. Make templates of his lesser minions so you 
will be able to produce them quickly and in number. Then plan out initial machinations and how the dark god 
will react to being thwarted, because the player characters are likely to prevent his initial efforts. Plan out how the 
conflict will escalate and be ready to improvise when things do not go as planned. 
Consultation: Now the player characters will have friends, advisors, lore givers and others they may have initially 
relied on in their low-title adventuring days and have now surpassed or reach parity with in the setting. These 
GMCs need to be ready to offer advice when asked without giving the whole plan to overcome the conflict to 
the characters or to overcome it for them. It is not that their competency suddenly fails. It is that the characters 
realize that those they looked up to before are fallible. They will see the limits of what they know and do not 
know. To overcome the conflict they may need the information these consultants have, or even some of their 
efforts in lesser matters, but with the player characters growing power, influence and knowledge it is they that 
will have to surpass their former mentors, friends and masters, leading the charge as the crusade marches on. 

===== PAGE 532 =====
526
Game Mastering
Go beyond recording what these great GMCs know and have control over. Add now their greatest weaknesses, 
the areas they are blind to and how they can fail. Use these against the GMCs, if necessary, as the conflict grows, 
so people the player characters have relied on in the past fail, or worse are lost to the conflict. This will leave 
the player characters more isolated and more in the spotlight to act and save the day. During this time many in 
the setting will be as the player characters once were, they will seek to consult with the player characters, to get 
advice, to be saved from harm, etc. It is important that the player characters are themselves now guiding others 
so that their roles grow as the conflict escalates. They should not just be more powerful characters but leaders 
as well. Not all will want or accept this roll nor should it be forced on all of them, but at least some in the party 
must have those they lead and protect, or the conflict will lose an important level of risk. Even if those under 
them are mere tools to power, losing them would involve losing power and so has consequences.
Epic, High Title Play: The important thing is to have growing danger at levels that threaten more than the lives 
of the player characters but the very people and lands they care about. Make sure to personalize any losses or 
triumphs, those they have saved from the conflict and those they have lost to it. Do not be afraid to kill a player 
character at this level if it is warranted. No matter how much time is invested, if the situation requires it, and 
especially if serious mistakes have been made a player character can die. It will only escalate the tension higher. 
It still isn’t you against them. It shouldn’t be done vindictively but as part of the process of escalating tensions as 
the conflict boils because mistakes were made and the consequences were known. There is sometimes a desire 
to just pick bigger creatures to fight and to make the battles bigger and more epic. To simply do this is to miss 
the more important points of epic, high-title play. It isn’t about slaying the dragon, it is about keeping the waking 
dragon from burning the countryside and despoiling all the player characters have lived in to this point. It is 
about stopping the fall of the civilization they grew up in. Or, it is about becoming part of the eternal conflict and 
making themselves known to the powers that be by thwarting some and aiding others. The players should now 
regularly have things to kept track of that if they ignore will begin to work against them or fail; spy networks, 
followers, strongholds, alliances, sponsored expeditions, other adventuring groups, etc. The success and failure of 
these efforts is now a central part of the tale even if the action happens out of play. No more should it be just the 
things they do directly but how what they have set in motion around them comes to pass. When it is time to fight 
the "bigger, badder" evil monster make sure to ease into it. Make it so that a direct, unplanned attack will simply 
fail. Planning, gathering the right tools, people and information should be as essential as the battle itself. Don’t 
be afraid that the battle will become anti-climactic because they will have done all this extra effort to chump 
the outcome. They will have earned that chumping. The battle being easier than they thought is the reward they 
have earned for all of their hard work and preparation.  Also the dice still have a factor. They may have removed 
much of the chance but there are still surprises left that the dice can bring. Maybe it is the apprentice in training 
that strikes the final blow. Perhaps a player character’s own weakness ends up being a strength at the right time, 
allowing them to triumph. They may have an irrational fear of spiders and so run from the early spider minions, 
they weren’t expecting, into a side room and find the levers that releases other planned surprises but this time 
against foes the party came to fight instead of against themselves at a later planned time. These happy accidents 
in the heat of the moment are not to be missed. They make the story unique and memorable. For instance, the 
magic Chetahl’s hat, that made the tent, that was used to throw the party, that thwarted the demonic assassin and 
ended the efforts of the demon to kill the party and start the cataclysm. All because the Chetahl liked a hat he 
saw on a deity and of all the absurd things focused on the hat during a rare and critical meeting with a god. This 
is how legends are born. They are carefully planned, set in motion, and then can be completely surprising when 
they actually happen. Embrace and extend it and the players will remember these times for years to come. 
Aftermath, Conclusions: When the conflict winds down. The "biggest, baddest" evil monster is defeated, the 
machinations of the dark god are ended and the seal set against any immediate reprisals, all the portals to the 
corrupting plane are closed and their armies beaten back and defeated, there will be consequences. Who and 
what was lost or given up for the final triumph? What now happens to the areas saved and those which had 
to be abandoned? Do the player characters now retire from the scene? Do they lead restoration efforts? What 
are the implications of the now weaker dark god? Does another god rise to take his place? Does the religion 
of the dark god falter, or go underground and become a cult? Does another kingdom or empire take this 

===== PAGE 533 =====
527
Game Mastering
moment of weakness to take over the civilization, or just spread their influence into it? Ask yourself as many of 
these questions as you can and answer them as part of the wrap-up. Make what the player characters did have 
consequences, both intended and unintended. In the preparation for the final session, create a write-up of these 
outcomes based on how the final events play out and then share with them these changes so that they have a true 
and earned ending. So that they are given the narrative they earned by having led a life of consequence and that 
this is known to one and all because the aftermath is shared by you. It isn’t that everything will be neatly wrapped 
in a bow. The seeds of the next conflict may even be in the conclusions of this one. But what will be revealed 
is what happened because of what they did and it will also create in their minds a sense of what might have 
happened had they chosen differently. If you as the GM do this right, the players will be thinking about it long 
after the final decision is made and the last die is cast. That is what it means for epic play. 
Warning: One final thought -- if it all comes apart, if the player characters fail and the world falls into chaos, go 
with it. Accept it. It will become a gaming cautionary tale for you and for them. Later triumphs will be made by 
this failure. Failure is the forge of victory. You will be tempted to smooth it all over; to have super being GMCs 
come in and fix the worst mistakes and save the world from the depredations of weak or chaotic players. Don’t 
give in to this. If you want to save the world, allow the cataclysm and create in the ashes a new hope. The second 
chance is with new characters (and if you must, new players) at the dawn of a new time. If you fix it for them 
you have denied them a life of consequence. Epic level play comes with risks, for you and for them. You may lose 
parts of your beloved setting that you have spent hours poring over, creating maps, GMCs and plots for, but this 
is the risk you agreed to take. It is a fidelity to the experience that you allow it to play out as it should. Don’t cheat 
yourself, or them. Let the bad endings happen. 
Beyond Epic Level: Life as an ascending or transcending being. 
This is the hardest play to pull off at all and should only be attempted when everyone is ready for the experience. 
All of the epic level efforts you have done in the past are ramped up; more minions, more followers, religions 
in your player character’s growing names, armies of allies and legions of plots and sub plots. There are new 
goals that seemed nigh on impossible just a few play sessions ago. Any contact with lesser beings is fraught 
with misunderstanding and unintended consequences. Actions must be deliberated upon more than simply 
done. Every session requires the GM to reflect on and create aftermaths. Lesser beings are looking to the 
player characters for more than their survival but to how they should live at all, or how to solve or resolve the 
greatest mysteries of the multiverse. Whether they answer to other sponsor gods as ascended beings or choose 
to transcend even other immortal beings to seek higher callings, they still are more and more connected to 
all around them, even as they rise above. It is paradoxical but true that as they have less and less contact with 
mortals and even other immortal beings what they do and say has even greater impact and so they are actually 
more connected. As the ascended or transcended player characters grow in power the setting evolves around 
them, even if they try to hide away from it. If care is not taken, a kind of action/reaction paralysis can set in 
or worse, a world-as-plaything to toy with and twist out of all proportion happens. At beyond epic levels the 
setting must and should defend itself against bad or inconsistent actors on its stage, not to save the setting from 
the players but because that becomes the pivot of play. What they want to do at this level becomes so hard that 
everything begins to resist it. Thus only the best, most well thought out decisions should have the traction 
necessary to make progress to their ultimate goals. While the world can be inextricably altered by a mere off-
hand comment it still should get them no closer to what they set out to achieve until the player characters find 
the flow of the setting and tune it in ways both subtle and grand to achieve the greatest of ends. Then what is 
their final reward? Perhaps they surpass their sponsoring god and now become a fixture in the setting. Or, they 
transcend completely and are given the final choice. Do you become one with all beings that were, are and will 
be, or do the leave it all behind to begin again and create a new multiverse. These are the final outcomes and past 
which no decision should or can be made. Such things should rarely or maybe even never happen but remain as 
the impossible goals.

528
Game Mastering

===== PAGE 535 =====
529
Game Mastering
Strongholds
As characters advances into the upper titles and gain 
renown, some will want to lay down roots in local 
communities, or create entire new communities or 
organizations around themselves and their ideals. From 
the burned-out warehouse rogue’s base deep in the city to 
the ruined keep in monster infested wildlands, each will 
have a beginning. Where they will end up will depend 
on time, effort, and a little luck. The stronghold system 
allows the aspiring character to create and maintain a 
stronghold, and watch it grow far beyond a simple base of 
operation. Running a stronghold is like running a business, 
there are many factors that lead to success or failure and 
all must be planned for, managed, and deftly handled. 
Ultimately, where it ends up will depend on the character’s 
focus, determination, and the conditions the stronghold is 
subject to. What happens is open-ended, whether that’s a 
system of guilds throughout a country, or a whole new city, 
anything is possible. A lone keep will require only a fraction 
of the material, while a city might use all of it. There are 
many additional usages, like determining local economic 
conditions and growth, or random GMC/extra encounters, 
etc. You will also be able to send your followers on missions 
to benefit the stronghold and its owner. A great deal of 
material is provided herein. Use as much of it, or as little as 
desired. Not everyone wants to deal with all the details. So, 
the GM can summarize, set a basic detail, and then handle 
the rest, leaving the player with simple decision making. Or 
the player may revel in the detail and want to micromanage 
it all. Use this expansion to fulfill either need. 
Part One: Acquisition
There are several steps in acquiring a stronghold. The 
character chooses the type to be established, the GM rolls/
determines condition, location, and current inhabitants. 
If the stronghold has a current legal owner, then it must 
be purchased, acquired legally, or otherwise from the 
owner. Even if it is owned it may be infested or inhabited 
by squatters that have to be cleared before it can be said to 
be acquired. Once the stronghold is occupied and cleared 
by the character and his allies or followers, it is considered 
acquired. 
Starting a Stronghold: This begins the process of acquiring 
and maintaining the stronghold. The character needs to 
make this intention known to the GM so the process can 
begin. At 7th title (name title) situational tables are rolled 
or chosen normally. For every title below 7th the situational 
tables should be rolled at -10% or (if choosing from the table 
as GM) you are strongly encouraged to lower one result 
lower for each title on the tables found in the acquisition 
section only. For every title above 7th add +10% to the rolls 
on situational tables or choose one result higher per title, if 
choosing as a GM. Again, this applies to the tables found in 
the acquisition part of strongholds only. 
Choosing the Stronghold Type: The first step is selecting 
the stronghold type desired. The character chooses the 
type of stronghold they are searching for and then the GM 
rolls or determines the conditions, steps to acquire it, etc. 
Stronghold is a broad word to describe anything from a 
wilderness protected by the character and their allies, to 
founding a city. 
Type
Wilderness Area/Park
Trade Route/Roadway

Guildhall/League House
Fighting Hall/Barracks
Temple/Monastery

Mage Tower/Academy

Combination of above
Condition of the Stronghold: The condition determines 
whether the stronghold exists already, must be rebuilt, or 
restored. Perhaps it is already owned and the owner must 
be convinced to part with it, or it is completely abandoned 
just waiting for the new owner to come along and make 
of it what they will.  This is rolled or chosen by the Game 
Master for the character. If anything besides non-existent 
is determined the GM will dictate how it came to be so, as 
background.

Game Mastering
Part Two: Repair and Maintenance
Once the character has made it to the stronghold, cleared or managed all infestations or inhabitants and claimed it through 
deed or by establishing residence within, then the next phase beings. Also, leader characters may return to this phase if their 
stronghold has been damaged. Depending on the stronghold condition, repairs or a whole rebuild may be required. 
Repair Costs: The costs to repair will vary but the costs are based around the material costs for building portions as shown 
in the equipment section of the Master’s Manual as well as prevailing labor and service costs. Labor costs can be reduced or 
eliminated by the character and/or his allies and followers performing the labor if they are qualified. Without specialized 
labor the results may be substandard, fail immediately, or over time and cause a structural collapse. One good laborer or 
specialist can direct up to five other non-skilled laborers, and still produce competent repairs based on their skill and not 
the skill of the laborers. If the skilled labor or specialist has Administration, they can direct 5 more individuals. If they have 
Leadership, they can direct 10 more for a possible maximum of 20 individuals directed and still produce results based on 
their skill.
Repair Time: Each 5 square feet of wall, roof, or floor of building repair requires one laborer who is skilled or directed by 
a specialist who is skilled in that material to repair. It will take twice as long for reinforced areas and three times as long for 
artistic or aesthetically pleasing areas. 
Clearing of Brush/Landscaping: Heavy brush requires an hour per 5 square feet per person. Light brush can be cleared at 
rate of 1 hour per 10 square feet per person. Landscaping can be done at rate of 1 hour per 20 square feet per person using 
Florist/Horticulturist, Planting/Harvesting, or Botanist. Maintenance takes 1 hour (once per week) per 10 square feet and 
can be done by anyone regardless of skill. 
Clearing of Hazards: This will vary by hazard and may require special skills. Perhaps the temperature is beyond humanoid 
norms, then a control weather spell, power or skill would be required to raise or lower the temperature within the required 
range. There could also be a poison plant infestation or a disease. Each would require intervention and the time to clear will 
vary by the hazard. Some examples are noted below but this is by no means an exhaustive list.

Part Four: Followers and the Protectorate
Once the character has adequate shelter, they may attempt to draw people to their stronghold. These fall into two general 
categories. 
Followers: These are the people that have pledged themselves directly to the stronghold owner and their service either 
directly or through long term direct employment. If there are not paid and merely fed and housed then they are referred 
to as minions. Those who defend the stronghold are guards or protectors, and any acting in the role of, or instead, of the 
owner to collect taxes, administer to the stronghold, prosecute criminals, or adjudicate hearings are considered officials 
of the stronghold. All of these are followers of the stronghold owner. Followers are directly or indirectly managed by the 
stronghold owner and as such are handled through morale rules from the Master’s Manual. Low morale will cause defection 
of followers. High morale will help attract more. Followers do not pay taxes, fees, or suffer burdens other than their service 
to the stronghold owner and the observance of the all applicable laws. 
Protectorate: Everyone who is not a follower is part of the protectorate. Including the family of followers, hired laborers, or 
service providers, whose only allegiance is to the coin they are paid, etc. Also, within this group are people that have moved 
into the stronghold (or area) and pay through tax, rent, harvest portions, or other services they provide. The protectorate 
form a single faction within the stronghold and the owner (and his administration) maintains a faction rating with the 
protectorate. If it gets too low the protectorate will leave the stronghold (or area). If it is high additional beings hear of 
the stronghold and will arrive and join the protectorate so long as there are places for them. In some cases, they will even 
construct their own homes and add to the stronghold, especially if it is a village, town or city. Visitors are considered part 
of the protectorate while they are visiting. Although they have their own reaction and may be part of other factions, faction 
modifiers effecting the protectorate will affect faction with visitors as well. 
Initial Followers: When a stronghold is acquired and cleared of previous unmanaged inhabitants/creatures (hazards 
can still exist) the word will get out and followers will arrive, drawn by the tales of the stronghold owner’s exploits. Some 
inhabitants found in the stronghold before it was acquired can become followers during play. If so add them to these 
numbers. These initial followers are not counted in the tables below but also fall into this category. The number and type 
of new followers attracted is shown as below and will arrive within the month of the stronghold being cleared. Some will 
require payment; others will pledge themselves and their lives to the cause. Use the table below to determine initial follower 
numbers and the tables that follow to determine type and makeup of followers.

Converting visitors to followers: Some visitors will have a very positive reaction to the stronghold owner or the stronghold 
administration. If the faction modifiers accrued during the visit (including the initial reaction) amount to +3 or higher 
than the visitor can be persuaded to stay. If the faction modifier amounts to +7 then once per month an attempt to convert 
the visitor to a follower can be made. The conversion occurs if a double Affinity roll is made by the stronghold owner, or a 
Diplomacy/Leadership skill roll by the stronghold’s administration is made. Failure indicates that the visitor will stay but 
is not yet convinced. Further attempts may be made in subsequent months as long as the faction bonus remains at +7 or 
higher. If three failures occur the visitor will leave. If the visitor is in a group, they will take the remainder of their group 
with them (minus any that have already pledged service). If the faction rating reaches maximum (+10) then conversion 
double Affinity or Diplomacy/Leadership skill rolls are made at +20% and as are the roll on the requirements for continued 
service table, increasing the likelihood of life-long service. Any number of visitors can be converted to followers as long as 
they have been in residence for a minimum of one month. 
Designating guards: A stronghold requires a minimum of 2 bodyguards for the stronghold owner which can be designated 
from amongst the followers. If the stronghold has protectorate (non-follower occupants) then a force of additional guards 
amounting to 5% of the total population of protectorates is required. These must also be designated from amongst followers. 
If there are not enough followers to form the required guard, then mercenaries may be hired to fill the remaining gap. 
Hiring mercenaries reduces protectorate faction by -2 and morale among other followers by 10%. This penalty is removed 
when the mercenaries are discharged. If the number of protectorate increases in a given month the stronghold has one 
additional month to increase the number of guards before being considered in an under-guarded state. 
Under-guarded: A stronghold is considered under-guarded if there are less than 2 body guards for the owner, and a guard 
force numbering under 5% of the protectorate population, or less than 1 guard per square mile. When under-guarding 
occurs then the following happens. Once in each stronghold event period there is an increase of crime chance, and once per 
month there is an increase in chance of attack. Use the tables below when the stronghold is under-guarded. The first month 
of acquisition of a stronghold it is exempt from the unguarded status.

New Protectorate Wealth: New protectorate will come with different levels of wealth and ability to improve their lives. 
While they may come to the stronghold or area with a different set of skills, their family background determines what 
wealth they come with. Sometimes the child of a nobleman will leave their family behind and seek adventure even if 
they themselves are not adventurers, or they may wish to escape their past. These incidents accounts for the very small 
percentage of nobles that find their way into a stronghold’s protectorates. They may not make their noble background 
known directly, but the money they bring with them and their spending will soon be felt.

Homesteading: Given the opportunity, some new protectorates will build their own homes, or improve upon the 
stronghold’s protectorate area by adding to existing structures. Setting a cost to rent or own land, or to homestead will 
reduce the number of attempted improvements or builds, but will reduce failures so a careful balance should be set. The 
stronghold owner collects directly any amounts paid to homestead or begin leasing a lot. If it is considered a lease then 1% 
to 5% of the initial lease price may be collected annually on tax/harvest day (see also resources, trade, and taxation). Failures 
noted below include structural failures, failures in ability to prosper enough to maintain the property, or might be in the

Calculating Total Protectorate: The total number of protectorates then is as follows: all free protectorates that are living 
within the stronghold or its area of control, plus, any currently hired protectorates to complete repair, expansions, or 
additional labor or services. Subtracting any protectorate loses that occurred in the month and finally any visitors are added 
to this number. After totaling this number, a new check is required to see if there are enough guards to support and police 
the protectorate (10% or more). See designating guards above. 
Population: The total population of the stronghold and its protected area is number of followers + number of protectorate + 
the owner.
Part Five: Improvements
Once the stronghold has been repaired, cleared, or made whole, improvements can be made. 
Improvement Costs: The costs for improvements will vary but the costs are based around the material costs for building 
portions as shown in the equipment section of the Master’s Manual as well as prevailing labor and service costs. Labor costs 
can be reduced or eliminated by the character and/or his allies and followers performing the labor if they are qualified. 
Without specialized labor the results may be substandard or fail immediately or over time and cause a structural collapse. 
One good laborer or specialist can direct up to five other non-skilled laborers and still produce competent improvements 
based on their skill and not the skill of the laborers. If the skilled labor or specialist has Administration, they can direct 5 
more individuals. If they have Leadership, they can direct 10 more for a possible maximum of 20 individuals directed and 
still produce results based on their skill.
Build Time: Each 5 square feet of wall, roof or floor of building improvement requires one laborer who is skilled or directed 
by a specialist who is skilled in that material to improve. It will take twice as long for reinforced areas and three times as long 
for artistic or aesthetically pleasing areas. 
Creation of New Landscaping: Landscaping can be done at rate of 1 hour per 20 square feet per person using Florist/
Horticulturist, Planting/Harvesting, or Botanist. Maintenance takes 1 hour (once per week) per 10 square feet and can be 
done by anyone regardless of skill. 
Magical or Divine Improvements: These are available by skill, power, or ability either from the stronghold owner, one 
of their followers, or protectorate. If none of these have the skill desired, then availability for this type of improvement 
will require the hiring of someone who has the skill. See specialized labor costs in the Master’s Manual. Improvements 
include blessed or blasphemed areas, sacred or haunted groves, (all depending on alignment) and/or wardings and various 
protections to name a few. 
Major Improvements (size): Those improvements expanding the useable protectorate area within the stronghold or its 
area by more than 1/4 of the existing, increase morale with followers by 5% and faction standing with the protectorate and 
current visitors by +1. Only one such improvement per month provides benefits and size improvement bonuses expire on 
the anniversary of the owner’s acquisition of the stronghold. 
Community (protectorate) Improvements: Certain improvements completed by the stronghold provide additional benefits 
to the protectorate inhabitants and this increase the strongholds faction standing with the protectorate.

Notes: No faction modifier is given for improvements in progress, only when they meet the thresholds noted. Also, if the 
population grows the faction modifier may be lost if the threshold is no longer met. Expansions or additional improvements 
may be needed as the stronghold and protectorate area grows. Some of these improvements require specialized knowledge. 
Running water requires hydrology and knowledge of how to make either aqueducts or pipes and possibly some form of 
power for pumps (steam, water power (water wheel) or air power (wind mill). The structures above may not be actually 
separate from the stronghold itself. A library for instance could be built into a wing of a castle, utilizing existing space but 
repurposing it for one of the above reasons. Doing so requires half the usual build time as long as space is available. 
Part Six: Costs
Every stronghold has costs to operate. Each owner must feed most of its followers and house them. Maintenance and 
improvements have to be paid for. Each cost must be managed lest the stronghold fail. Many stronghold owners start 
with a ready supply of wealth from their adventures, but this can be quickly squandered in costs to followers and hireling 
protectorates for improvements. For economy we will start with fixed costs, work towards variable costs, and then move 
through fixed and variable resources available to produce a stronghold income. Use the tables below to determine and 
record these until you have a balance sheet of what it costs to run the stronghold from month to month and how much it 
either generated (in the black) or loses (in the red). Costs, together with resources and trade allow an economy to form. If a 
stronghold has a protectorate at all it will likely develop an economy based around these factors.
Fixed Costs: These are costs that remain from season to season, month to month, and must be paid to continue operating 
the stronghold. They create a baseline.
Stronghold Rent/Leasing: If the stronghold is within a kingdom or political body that requires a rent or lease to be paid on 
the land and/or structure, then this cost must be set aside to be paid or the stronghold will be foreclosed on and the owner 
evicted. Take the yearly amount of rent/lease and divide it by 12 to get the monthly costs. 
Yearly rent or leasing of land and/or structure  / 12 = monthly lease or rent. 
Stronghold Maintenance: Every stronghold from the simplest tavern to a city requires maintenance to keep it from 
following apart. Followers can be enjoined to complete these tasks if they have the requisite skills (stone masonry for 
stone structures, wood working for wooden ones, etc.) Even if the labor is free there is generally cost associated with the 
raw materials (stone, wood, metal) or finished pieces, doors, windows, fixtures, etc. Now it may be that these too can be 
provided by resources available within the stronghold. If so, the maintenance costs may be minimal, but the requirement 
in labor and goods should be noted regardless. In general, it costs 1/10th of 1% of the value of a stronghold in labor and 
goods to maintain that stronghold each month. While in a given month there may be no repairs, only cleaning, oiling, 

===== PAGE 554 =====
548
Game Mastering
etc., the average over time will be 1/10th of 1%. Increase this cost if is no non-stronghold owner food or housing, and 
the owner provides these to the required staff. To determine the number of staff involved, compare half of the monthly, 
non-catastrophic maintenance budget to costs of labor to see how many protectorate are required. If followers are being 
used, determine what the theoretical monthly budget would be for labor alone (1/2 of the budget.) and see how many of 
the correct type of labor are needed. Reminder of the makeup of the maintenance team is often 1 specialist for every 5 
(sometimes more) general laborer. See improvement for more details. 
There are two methods for dealing with maintenance. The first is doing no actual maintenance (other than general cleaning) 
and maintaining a repair fund (growing or capped) and then pay for staff and repair only as needed. The other is to allocate 
the money each month to pay a dedicated maintenance staff. Either method has its pros and cons. A fund is often the 
cheapest way but then the fund may not be enough to pay for catastrophic failures that can occur due to improper, or lack 
of, maintenance. Dedicated maintenance will often keep a catastrophic failure from occurring but in the rare cases it may 
not be enough in the maintenance budget to repair the damage, except over a long period of time.  Some stronghold owners 
maintain both a monthly maintenance budget and a catastrophic repair fund. Note these as fixed costs, although if the 
catastrophic fund is capped at a certain figure, it rolls off the fixed costs once it is capped until it is utilized and then it must 
be filled again. 
Events can also occur unrelated to maintenance that damages the stronghold (see events). These can either be absorbed over 
time in slow repairs with the monthly maintenance budget, or in a fast manner with the catastrophic repair fund. The choice 
is up to the stronghold owner. 
Monthly maintenance budget (1/10th of 1% of the value of the stronghold, half labor, half goods) and/or catastrophic repair 
fund monthly payments = monthly stronghold maintenance and repair fixed costs. 
Use the tables below dealing with the costs of general maintenance, small damage events, or catastrophic failures. Failure 
chances are rolled each month in addition to the normal events. Damaging events can also occur in addition to these (see

Follower Payroll: The cost of each follower is determined one month after they first arrive when they decide to offer their 
service, and while some will offer their services for free, most will not. Determine for each what the monthly total cost is 
and then total it. If followers are not paid, each must make a morale check each month, failure indicates they have left the 
owner’s service. Also, each follower that leaves (up to 4) reduce remaining follower morale by 5% for the following month. 
This modifier is removed as soon as all pay is paid and caught up. 

===== PAGE 556 =====
550
Game Mastering
Sum of each follower’s monthly cost = monthly total follower payroll fixed costs
Follower Room: For each follower there must be a place for them to sleep that must be kept repaired with amenities (jakes/
toilets, water, etc.) in good working order. This will amount to 1 silver per month per follower in normal circumstances. Add 
more for areas that require more resources, such as a cold environment where fire wood, coal, or charcoal must be burned to 
keep warm (doubling the cost) or half as much for lush areas where access to water is easy and temperatures do not have to 
be controlled, etc. Start with a silver per month per follower and add or subtract as appropriate for the conditions. Costs can 
be higher if the stronghold does not house its own followers, and must pay to house them in nearby structures not owned by 
the stronghold owner. 
Sum of each follower x 1 silver (plus any regional modifiers) = monthly total follower room fixed costs
Follower Board: Most followers must be fed. A few can feed themselves, either through hunting, farming or through some 
sort of magic or ability. As a rule of thumb, it will take 4 copper pieces per day to feed each follower who requires it, for a 
total of 1 gold 2 silvers per month in food costs. This can be a little less for scholarly (1 gold) or less active followers, and 
more for guards or strenuously active followers (1 gold 5 silvers). If the stronghold has farms then every 2 acres of wheat is 
enough to feed 1 average person for an entire year. Some of these costs may be reduced but you end up paying the farmer 
to grow the wheat or for the wheat. If the follower is the farmer and is listed as someone who does not need food as part of 
their conditions for being in service then you can deduct the cost of 1 follower’s yearly food for every 2 acres of farmland. 
But additional help will be needed at harvest time. At harvest time your variable costs will rise or your followers will have to 
be part of the harvesting team (see variable costs.)
Sum of each follower x (either 1 gold, 1.2 gold or 1.5 gold depending on activity) = monthly total follower board fix costs.
Total Monthly Follower Fixed Cost: Now you can take the follower monthly payroll, the monthly room and monthly board 
for total monthly follower fixed cost.  
Follower monthly payroll + follower monthly room costs + follower monthly board costs = total monthly follower fixed cost.  
Protectorate Payroll: Some of the protectorate are in fixed positions that are paid monthly. Perhaps they perform a service 
(such as local priest) for the stronghold, but have not pledged themselves as followers to its owner. Their costs must be 
calculated for the month, tallied up, and added to the protectorate fixed payroll cost. These costs are outlined in the Master’s 
Manual and should be added as fixed cost if they are in places of permanent employment within the stronghold. For others 
doing temporary work, including the initial repair and/or build out of the stronghold this is a variable cost and calculated 
there, see variable costs. If actual or economic slaves are used instead of a paid protectorate by a Neutral or Evil owner 
(depending on the society), then see room and board below for factional and protectorate faction modifiers. Note, slaves 
have their own faction separate from the stronghold’s free protectorate, but protectorate faction is affected by the treatment 
of slaves. A protectorate may see the difference between slavery and employment as a thin line and fear that they may 
themselves be mistreated, or at the very least are living in an unjust situation. 
Sum of each permanently paid protectorate’s monthly cost = monthly total protectorate payroll fixed costs
Protectorate Room and Board: Generally, protectorate hirelings including those that are on permanent staff are expected 
to pay for their own room and board out of their salary. The exceptions to this are when the stronghold owner is the only 
source of food and accommodations. Sure an owner can charge the protectorate additionally for the room(s) and food 
provided but doing so, while gaining short term economic benefit in recoup of some or all of salaries paid, has an immediate 
negative factional impact and a long term economic impact as the protectorate flee the employ of the stronghold owner for 
better opportunity elsewhere. Absorbing the costs for protectorate housing is 1 silver per month per housed protectorate 
(plus any regional modifiers due to conditions). Costs for food are 1 gold, 2 silvers per month per protectorate. Alternately 
the stronghold owner may be Neutral or Evil (depending on the society), and just use slavery to meet permanent needs, if 
so, their follower morale will suffer along with protectorate faction. 
Sum of each permanently paid protectorate’s room and board (if supplied) = monthly total protectorate room and board fixed 
costs
