Total Monthly Protectorate Fixed Cost: Now you can take the protectorate monthly payroll, the protectorate room and 
board, and arrive at the total monthly protectorate fixed cost.  
Permanently paid protectorate monthly payroll + permanently paid protectorate monthly room and board costs = total monthly 
protectorate fixed cost.  
Total Monthly Fixed Cost: Now that you know your strongholds rent or leasing costs, maintenance costs, fixed follower 
costs, and fixed protectorate costs, you can total these for the total monthly fixed costs. This is colloquially referred to as ‘the 
nut’ that has to be paid each month to keep the Stronghold operational and solvent.  
Monthly lease/rent + monthly stronghold maintenance and repair fixed costs + total monthly follower fixed cost + total monthly 
protectorate fixed cost = total monthly fixed cost.
Variable costs: These are one-time or temporary costs for stronghold improvements, training, mercenaries, militia call-up, 
and/or special projects. The key ingredient is their temporary nature. They add temporarily to the cost of maintaining the 
stronghold, although some improvements may require additional permanent staff, such as teacher(s) when a school/library 
is built. The cost of any of these is totaled and divided over the months it will take to complete them. Thus, if it will take 2 
and a half months to complete a library, then split the cost into three parts and add it to the variable costs for the next three 
months. 
Improvements: Required goods are calculated for the improvement (see Master’s Manual equipment: construction costs) 
and if not able to be provided by stronghold resources, then their costs are divided over the course of the build period. 
Labor needs are likewise determined, skilled followers may be able to provide the labor and required expertise, but under 
most conditions more protectorate needs to be hired to complete the project. Check to see what free protectorate are 
available at the stronghold, and hire these first at normal cost. After existing labor is factored in, protectorate must be hired 
from outside the stronghold to complete the improvement. As before, their housing and food costs are not always a concern 
if there is enough non-owner stronghold housing (see new protectorates). Total all of these factors and you have your 
improvement’s cost, divide by the member of months for the monthly variable cost.   
Required goods + required protectorate labor (and possibly room and board) / months to complete improvement = monthly 
improvements variable cost (in the months until the improvement is completed).  
Training: Offering training to protectorates and followers improves the capability of the Stronghold. The stronghold’s 
people are often its most important resource. Investing in training will improve what they can do and how many roles they 
can serve in or be hired for. Guards for instance can be made up of anyone in service to the stronghold owner who can 
reasonably swing a weapon. But sometimes more is called for, perhaps an external army or expeditionary force. Training 
the able boded protectorate into a well-ordered militia allows them to be called up to defend the stronghold in times of true 
emergency or war. But this takes time and not everyone succeeds. First a teacher with skills must be found, and if not, a 
follower paid to train. Food and housing sometimes have to be provided if the stronghold owner is the only source of these. 
If more than a few are to be trained, then more teachers have to be hired.  Use the following table for training purposes.

Notes: the social skill Instruction allays grants a +20% to the success rate. Each modifier skill possess by the teacher adds +5% 
more to the success rate with a maximum of 95% success rate. Monthly cost of the teacher increases by 1 gp. per month for each 
additional modifying skill, they have from the modifying skill list. Students who failed before get a +10% bonus to be retrained 
in the same skill set if they try again.  
Number of teachers for number of students to be trained x monthly cost for each * number of months (rounded up) to complete 
training = monthly training variable costs. 
Mercenaries: Usually hired in times of war or to reach the required number of guards to get the stronghold to a guarded 
state (guards equal to or exceeding 10% of the total population of protectorates population or less than 1 guard per square 
mile). As stated before, mercenaries make those around them uneasy. Hiring mercenaries reduces protectorate faction 
by -2, and morale among other followers by 10% for the duration of their stay. The cost per mercenary varies by the title, 
0 title weapon wielders, archers, shield bearers cost 5 gp. each per month.  Others (warriors, scouts, vary by title, 1st title 
classed-mercenaries are 10 gp. per month, and on up. see Master’s Manual, equipment: Hiring GM characters). Multi-
month contracts can be negotiated below this price but generally not below half unless in exception circumstances. In such 
negotiations mercenaries may ask for additional hazard pay or bonuses for their captains, etc. 
Sum of each mercenary’s monthly cost = Monthly mercenary cost.
Militia Call-up: In times of war or emergency able-bodied protectorate who have been militia trained can be called up. 
Generally, weapons have to be provided for them (sometimes at additional cost), and they have to be fed and housed in 
temporary housing during the crisis if the stronghold is larger than a single structure. Single structure (or very small) 
strongholds (less than a dozen structures) militia call ups, can have the militia returning home for food and shelter on 
nights they are not on duty, unless those militia are being sent out to fight a threat. Militia can be asked to do this for free 
for no more than 1 week, over this they will generally expect to be paid for their lost wages at rate of 3 gp. per month (2 gp. 
if they are fed and housed). Failure to do so will lower their morale by 10% for each month of non-pay and cause a 20% 
desertion rate. Although militia are usually part of the protectorate they do not use faction while serving, but morale as if 
they were followers. This is useful as morale is what is checked in combat situations, not faction standing. 
Sum of each militia’s monthly cost (including any weapons, temporary food and housing) = Monthly militia call-up cost.
Special Projects: These require special skills, such as the locator skills (prospector, hunting, etc.) to find resources in the 

===== PAGE 559 =====
553
Game Mastering
Stronghold’s protected area. Only the cost of hiring the specialists is needed to complete a special project. In some cases, 
these costs are borne by using followers to complete them. If no followers have the requisite skill(s), check to see what free 
protectorate are available at the stronghold, and hire those at normal cost. After existing labor is factored in, protectorate 
must be hired from outside the stronghold to complete the improvement. As before their housing and food costs are not 
always a concern, if there is enough non-owner stronghold housing (see new protectorates). Total all of these factors and 
you have your special project’s cost, divide by the member of months for the monthly variable cost. Some special projects 
are ongoing (such as the hunting for resources, see below for success and additional costs).
Required protectorate labor (and possibly room and board) / months to complete special project = monthly special projects 
variable cost (in the months until the special project is operational).

Notes: Reducing the chance of an event means if that event occurs then there is a chance the event was prevented. So, if there are 
3 scouts per square mile and the scouts are set to search for dangerous humanoids, then the dangerous humanoid event occurs 
and there is a 60% chance (20 x 3) that the intrusion did not occur. This is because the scout found the intruders and protectors 
were dispatched to repel them without incident. Thus, the event was stopped before it became a threat to the stronghold. If the 
event was a disease outbreak, physicians might need to be deployed. In the cases were the community had neither physicians, 
nor healers, the event still occurs. Success is the chance of the resource or resource location being found (see resources). Failure 
is cumulative. Thus, if a failure occurs it means that resource is no longer available in area of the stronghold. If renewable it will 
not return unless repopulated by outside influence. 
Total Monthly Variable Costs: This is the total additional costs the stronghold administration is carrying in a given month. 
It includes the costs of improvement projects, training, militia call up, and special projects. This total will likely vary from 
month to month unlike the more stable fixed costs. 
Monthly improvements variable cost+ monthly training variable costs + monthly militia call-up cost + monthly special projects 
variable cost = total monthly variable costs.
Total Monthly Cost: This is the total outgo in a given month that the stronghold pays. It includes everything that comes out 
of the coffers that month both fixed and variable. 
Total monthly fixed cost + total monthly variable costs = total monthly costs.
Part Seven: Resources, Taxation, and Trade
The economic situation in a stronghold can seem pretty bleak when you are managing the month-to-month costs. But 
not to worry, most strongholds have opportunities to make money. If the stronghold has protectorate then they have skills 
and the output of these skills is goods and services, and those can be taxed. Also, if the stronghold is more than just a 
single structure, resources may be available to offset costs. While these goods, services, and any raw resources increase the 
potential for trade, shrewd traders can make money just from the buying and selling of goods and services. 
Together these factors will go to make up an economy.  That economy may benefit the stronghold owner, their followers, 
or all of the inhabitants depending on how it is managed. A carefully managed economy can grow until its influence is far 
beyond the stronghold itself. Much depends on the economic resources of the stronghold, and the people who live within 

===== PAGE 560 =====
554
Game Mastering
it. Over taxing these could cause protectorates to flee or provide fewer services. Not taxing them may provide less ability to 
make improvements or to prepare for calamitous events. A balance must be sought and carefully maintained to create long 
term growth for the stronghold and the owner’s wealth. 
Identifying Resources: Some resources are created directly, such as basic food from planting and growing. Some are the 
services offered by the people of the stronghold. Others have to be found, collected, refined, made into simple goods, or 
made into more complex or artistic goods. Land or structures leased to the protectorate or third parties allow the stronghold 
(or its environs) to become a resource. Selling goods and services itself can be a resource if properly managed.

Collecting Resources: When a resource is grown (domesticated animals/crops) or a special project uncovers a resource 
batch, then the resource can be harvested with the appropriate harvesting skill, until that batch or location of the resources 
is depleted. Continued collection of that resource in many cases ends when the resource is no longer available within the 
controlled area of the stronghold. If the resource is renewable, and is carefully managed, then this balance means less 
immediate profit, but long-term profit is greatly enhanced. Below are tables to help identify the richness and value of found 
resources, and how long they can be utilized before another such resource can be found.

Trade and Competition: Trade can be the life blood of even a small stronghold. If the stronghold owner offers any goods or service 
directly, then it can dampen the market for protectorate merchants and traders. The stronghold owner may wish to stay out of the 
direct market, or choose only a few key markets. The owner may run several projects to find resources, and then charge a fee for the 
exploitation of the found resources. Or the owner could own the entire chain from finding the resources, extracting them, refining 
them, crafting goods, or finishing them, to finally selling them within the stronghold, trading them to neighbors, or others along 
a trade route. If the labor and tools used are paid or owned by stronghold owner, then all the profit (after labor) belongs to the 
stronghold owner. A very common practice is to pick a renewable resource and a non-renewable one, and create a local monopoly 
for each. Then allow all other goods and services to be sold with a small 3-5% taxation rate, allowing for a healthy balance between 
guaranteed income for the stronghold, and supporting a market economy for other goods and services among the protectorate. 
Setting up Shop:  Special projects to find resources, labor to extract it, refine it, and create the goods finished or otherwise are 
shown in previous steps and in the Master’s Manual under labor costs. It comes down to sales - total costs = profit. A shop costs 1 
merchant to run per 1000’ square feet. Sales will depend on the price set, the available consumer base, and the amount of goods to 
sell. These factors are outlined below.

Game Mastering
Nearby Competition and Markets: If a nearby community (within 1 week’s travel) sells a product that is the same or close 
to a product that is sold in the stronghold, or its environs, then the prices will drop, unless the price is higher at the nearby 
community. There is a -10% penalty to sales conditions on a particular good for each community within one week, that 
sells the item for less than the stronghold. Availability of resources can also impact the cost of a good or resource by -5% for 
each nearby community that has the resource. Alternately, anything that the stronghold is selling, from resources to finished 
goods that is sold for a lower price (or is simply not available) in nearby communities then traders will buy the resource or 
good from the stronghold, increasing market conditions. 
Market Condition
Stronghold Sales Modifier (for this good)
Each nearby community that sales the good at a lower price than the stronghold
-10%
Each nearby community that supplied a resource needed for the good
-5%
Each nearby community that does not have a stronghold resource
+5%
Each nearby community that sales the good at a higher price than the stronghold
+5%
Each nearby community that does not have the gods sold at a stronghold.
+10%
Trade Routes and Sea Lanes: There are two ways that trade routes and sea lanes can form. One is by special project. The 
stronghold owner pays for 2d4 guards, 1d4+1 wagons, 1-2 merchant, 1 cook, and a guide, to create a trade route, or 1 
trading vessel, its crew and complement of marines to create a sea lane to the nearest community. This takes a month to 
establish, or double the travel time, whichever is longer. 
The trade route (or sea lane) can then be extended by hiring a second team (or crew) to extend the trade route from the 
nearby settlement to another settlement even farther away. The route or lane cannot take longer than 1 year to make a round 
trip on. The benefit of trade routes and sea lanes is every connected community on the route or lane is considered a nearby 
community for resources, goods and services, see Nearby Competition and Markets above.
The second way that trade routes can form is through the protectorate creation of trading houses. They sometimes create 
their own new trading routes and sea lanes without the direction of the Stronghold or its owner. The stronghold gains 
benefits from these whether they were created by the stronghold owner or the protectorate, see non-stronghold Owner 
Shops.
Part Eight: Missions
From the moment the Stronghold is established the owner beings to amass followers. These followers, and paid protectorate 
(hirelings), and even incentivized protectorate can be sent, or encouraged to go on missions to aid the stronghold, its owner, 
and/or themselves. Some missions can be completed with one person, but most will require teams and the better trained 
the more likely to succeed. While anyone can scout, a trained ranger or border scout will likely be able to do so undetected, 
and see things many would miss. Likewise sending only soldiers on trade mission, or scouts on a diplomatic mission will 
likely lead to failure. The outcome of the mission will depend on many factors besides the group’s makeup. If the territory 
is dangerous then guards will be needed to counter any threats while traveling. Success or failure itself can be partial and 
nuanced, some objectives completed while parts are missed. Even complete failures may sometimes be recovered from, 
by sending an additional rescue mission with the right resources. Choose the mission type, build a team, and set them on 
it, and the GM will determine what the applicable chances are, and the outcome, which will resolve in an upcoming event 
window depending on the mission. 
Mission Selection and odds determination: The mission type is selected and the generally desired outcome is described. 
Then the team is selected and sent on the mission. Mission length is determined by the Game Master based on the described 
desired outcome, and then outcome encounter and mishap chances are determined. Each of these is rolled for each of the 
event periods during the mission, and then outcome determined by mission type. If the Stronghold owner gets reports, they 
get word of how the mission is going in that event period. As long as none of the mishaps or encounters end the mission, it 
continues until the last event period is rolled for. Then the mission outcome chance is rolled for the final result. The mission 
type is consulted and the outcome determined, which is then reported on in the next stronghold event period when the 
mission team returns and reports (or their outcome is known).

Mission Results for Each Event Period and Final Outcomes: During each event period the mission will run encounter 
chances and mission mishaps. If either or both occurs, then consult the mission types below for further determination. 
When the final event period is reached, roll one final time for encounters, mishaps, and then roll for overall mission success 
based on all the factors collected in the tables above. If casualties occur roll for each casualty on the casualty table. If more 
than half the team is incapacitated, then the mission cannot continue and is considered a failure. If they are instructed to 
continue no matter what, morale checks must be made to continue by each individual member, unless a leader rallies them.

Part Nine: Turns
Once ownership of the stronghold is established, and initial events and conditions are determined and/or overcome, it is 
time to begin stronghold turns if the stronghold is to be managed in periods of time outside of normal game time (day-to-
day). The GM and player establish a timeline for when the turns will begin, and what each turn period will be (1 month, 
2-weeks, etc.) The GM provides all of the main stronghold forms filled out with information so the player can begin 
managing their new stronghold. These forms also include the initial events the stronghold owner will respond to; visitors, 
crimes, etc. A blank turn sheet is provided to the player.
General Details: The player describes the general state of their stronghold here, its location, and how their character sees it. 
Provide the date of the turn start above and the agreed upon turn period above and right. 
Turn Costs: The player takes the information provided, determines how much their costs will be for the turn period, marks 
that cost in the turn sheet, and removes that amount from their fortune. If they do not have enough money then decisions 
will have to be made; reduce staff, release mercenaries, sell off something, etc.  Mark these costs as paid on the turn form 
and add any cost decisions in the next section (decisions).
Decisions: This will section will already have the details of any decisions made because of costs.  Now the proud owner of 
the stronghold makes their general decisions. How to punish criminals, changes in tax rate, setting up of homesteads for 
new arrivals, how to treat visitors, general decrees, etc. This is where the player will provide details about how they lead the 
stronghold. 
Improvements/Upgrades/Repairs: In this section repairs are made, or improvements/upgrades from additional money. 
Add these costs to the general turn costs in the first section. These are over and above general maintenance, staff costs, etc. 
Owner Activities/Missions: The owner and their established party, or the owner and their main group of followers outline 
any mission or activities planned. This includes adventures, missions, training, etc. 
Follower Activities/Missions: Here the owner establishes what groups or individuals will be doing in the turn period; 
including missions, training, changes in duty, etc. 
Other: Here add additional follower/group missions, or details that overran any of the previous sections, or that don’t 
generally fit in a particularly category but may be noteworthy. Also use this area for notes or questions to the GM. 
Notes: Supply the GM with your completed turn sheet. They will then give a new event sheet and any updated sheets due to 
changes from the turn. 

===== PAGE 595 =====
589
Game Mastering
Stronghold Play
The general idea of stronghold play is to give a character a chance to retire from day-to-day adventuring, and live the life 
of someone of consequence who has earned their way in the world as an individual, and now wants to lead from a place 
of strength, the stronghold. Play should continue for as long as both the GM and player are satisfied with it. It can even be 
interwoven in with the ongoing world story in such a way that the player feels their character is still making an impact on 
the world events, even though they are no longer day-to-day adventuring. Alternately, they can continue their adventuring 
life but make frequent trips to their stronghold to make decisions and assure all is going smoothly. Turns may occur 
between adventures or during them. Whatever the GM and players agree to. Hopefully, the sense of a character who has 
earned their place in the world will be strongly felt, and the satisfaction that can bring will deepen and increase fulfillment 
of play.

final necessary to garner those values. In many settings magic gained is considered its own reward and not worthy of 
additional gain. There are times for instance when a rogue acquires a magic item through theft or deception that even 
in such settings they should be worth a value. It is recommended that if experience compensation is given that it not 
be the gold piece value of the magic item (which can be extraordinary) but the values listed here.

New Creature Abilities 
360-degree vision: When vision is 360 degrees chance to be 
Surprised is reduced by 100%. Cost: 10 PP (5 if combined 
with extra eyes).
Absorptive Skin: The creature’s skin absorbs nutrients doing 
1d4 acid damage to exposed flesh per minute, dissolving it. 
Cost: 5 PP.
Acid Skin: The skin of the creature is acidic and lowers the 
object strength of objects that touch it, as well as damaging 
flesh (but not the creature itself). This will apply to any 
objects which touch the creature. Cost: 5 PP per 1d10 of 
damage.
Aura Sense: The creature has the ability to sense the Aura 
rating of other creatures, Aura magics, as well as active 
spells. Cost: 5 PP.
Air Bladder (Magical): A large bladder within or on the 
body that stores air for very long periods, even multiplying 
available air through magical means. The bladder is 
considered invulnerable to pressure changes. Cost: 7 PP.
Air Jets (Magical): the ability to magically condense air and 
eject it at high speed and volume in a continuous fashion for 
fast propulsion. Cost: 7 PP.
Beam, Death: A death ray that travels 10 feet per level of the 
creature. Any being struck must make a Magic Resistance or 
die instantly. Cost: 100 PP.
Beam, Fire: A heat ray that travels 10 feet per level of the 
creature. Any being struck must make a Magic Resistance or 
take 1d6 damage per level of the creature. Cost: 25 PP.
Beam, Paralysis: Shoots a beam of paralysis that goes 10 
feet per level of the creature. Any being struck must make 
a Magic Resistance or be paralyzed for 10 seconds per 
creature level. Cost: 15 PP.
Beam, Sleep: A sleep ray that travels 10 feet per level of the 
creature. Any being struck with less than 15 Will Force must 
make a Control Resistance or fall asleep for 1 minute per 
level of the creature. Cost: 10 PP.
Breathing Skin: Breathes through its skin, instead of lungs 
or gills. Cost: 2 PP.
Chameleon Skin (or Fur): The creature has a skin which will 
change to the color of the environment around it. Evoke: 
+20% to Blend, +10% to Move Unseen. Cost: 5 PP.
Chaos Skin: The skin of the creature has a magical chaos 
effect and lowers the object strength of objects that touch it, 
as well as damaging flesh (but not the creature itself). This 
will apply to any objects which touch the creature. Cost: 8 
PP per 1d12 of damage.
Compound Eyes: Vision is extended in a hemispherical 
pattern but clarity is reduced. -1 melee/-2 missile attack but 
chance to be surprised is reduced by 50%. Cost: 0 PP.
Control Voice: When a victim hears the voice of the 
creature, the victim must make a Control Resistance or fall 
under the effects of the spell Control Humanoid as long as 
the victim can hear the voice. Cost: 12 PP.
Dead Changeling Form: Being can change into another 
humanoid form twice per day if it has touched the 
targeted dead being it wants to appear as. Applying the 
racial modifiers for that race, against the Changeling’s 
original values changes physical attributes and Appearance 
accordingly. The Disguise skill allows the Changeling to 
assume the form of a particular individual of that race. The 
Mimic skill allows the Changeling to speak as a particular 
individual. Cost: 50 PP.
Destroy Divinity: The being’s touch can dispel Divinity 
at 10% per level of the being versus the effect. (5% x Piety 
Control or 10% per title/level of the being making the 
effect.) Cost: 25 PP.
Destroy Magic: The being’s touch can dispel magic at 10% 
per level of the being versus the effect. (5% x Aura Control 
or 10% per title/level of the being making the effect.) Cost: 
25 PP.
Divine Isolation: Being cannot use, create, or be the focus of 
divine magical skills and invocations. Cost: 50 PP.
Divine Sense: The ability to sense divine magic, active 
invocations, or supernatural beings. Cost: 5 PP.
Constriction: Has limbs or tendrils that can constrict. Cost: 
5 PP.
Cloud Emitter: This creature emits an obscuring cloud, 
+20% to Surprise Attack, Move Unseen. Is -2 to be hit. Cost: 
10 PP.
Darts: The creature can fire darts whose damage is based on 
creature size (as claws).
Dormant State (Perfect): As Dormant State, but no 
Endurance is lost. Cost: 30PP.
Dream Slay: This creature’s attack can kill creatures on the 
dream plane or who are illusionary in nature. If the victim 
is an illusion or a dreamer projected onto the dreamscape, 
they have to make a Magic Resistance for each attack or 
they are killed. Dreamer projections are sent back to their 
plane of origin and must make a Will Force save or suffer a 
heart attack (see Master’s Manual). If the victim is actually 
present in the dreamscape, then this effect can actually kill 
permanently if a Magic Resistance fails but only natural to 
hit rolls of 21 – 1 per 2.5 creature levels or titles or use the 
table below. Cost: 20PP.

to understand that the being is split into three parts and
